# §G — Persistence, namespaces, query contracts, and recovery boundaries
**CHD-3.4 · SPEC V3.4. REVISION NOTICE — supersedes CHD-3.3.** This section specifies required storage safety properties. It does not select a complete deployable writer protocol. G-12 remains OPEN for versioned LeaseAuthority/FencedStore/SnapshotToken transport, persistence, wrapper/key migration and historical membership. §21 prints the actual pinned memory-HTTP mapping and its reference-only variant catalog. Neither an external pre-write lease check nor a local SQLite transaction supplies atomic storage-boundary fencing. All algorithms below are requirements conditional on that binding, not capabilities demonstrated by DuckBrain.

## G.1 Namespaces and the substrate boundary
The controller is the only `/chd/*` writer. Agents use authorized controller operations and never receive a DuckBrain write token. The archive ingestor alone writes `/sessions/*` and `/gaps/*`. Project/code memory is a separate, eventual namespace and is never evidence that a control-plane write committed.
DuckBrain is an append-only, multi-version key/value surface. It provides per-write durability when the response says `X-Durability: fsync`; it does **not** provide a transaction spanning two keys, a compare-and-set on an append-only key, a room order, or an authoritative latest version. The controller therefore uses two required adapters:
* **`LeaseAuthority`** requires linearizable acquire/renew/takeover and a monotone `fence_epoch`. No backend is selected here. A DuckBrain read-then-write or an independent lease service checked before an unfenced append is not an implementation. The lease and storage-boundary authority must be coupled atomically by the versioned G-12 binding. * **`FencedStore`** is the only write adapter. Every append carries `(owner_id, boot_id, fence_epoch, write_id)` and the adapter atomically checks that the lease authority still owns that fence before accepting the append. If the deployment cannot make that check part of the authoritative write path, readiness fails `fencing_unavailable`; the controller refuses all writes rather than relying on a best-effort pre-check.
A successful constituent append means: request accepted by the adapter, `X-Durability: fsync`, and an exact readback matching the canonical bytes and `write_id`. A response without all three is `unknown`, not success. Git debounce, S3, replication, and wake delivery are downstream outputs with separate status; none is a commit point.
TABLE 7.1-1 — G.1 Namespaces and the substrate boundary
| Class | Namespace | Examples | Visible only when | |---|---|---|---| | control/coordination | `chd` | requests, journal, rooms, heads, manifests, grants, tickets, reports, datasets, audit | a valid commit marker covers the record and every constituent readback passes | | session archive | `chd-archive` | export payload, manifests, gaps, indexes | archive commit marker covers payload and manifest/index | | project memory | deployment-defined | observations and code knowledge | its own eventual checkpoint; never a control acknowledgement |

## G.2 Record envelope and authoritative state
Every append is a canonical JSON envelope with `schema_version`, `record_id`, `key`, `rev`, `commit_seq`, `written_by`, `request_id`, `write_id`, `tx_id`, `fence_epoch`, `state`, and a canonical `payload`. `canonical_bytes` means UTF-8 JSON with sorted object keys, no insignificant whitespace, and deterministic number/string encoding. The digest is SHA-256 over those bytes. Timestamps are descriptive audit fields only.
The following records are authoritative; local boards, response prose, logs, and caches are mirrors:
* `RequestClaim` records the logical request and immutable request digest. It is the idempotency authority and is written before any business record. * `JournalIntent` records the ordered constituent list, expected keys, expected digests, and operation preconditions. It is the recovery authority for an in-flight compound operation. * `CommitMarker` is the visibility gate. It lists every constituent `(key, write_id, digest)` and is written last. A marker is valid only if it is durable, has the current fence, has a matching intent, and every listed constituent is read back byte-identically with `state=prepared`. * `ResponseRecord` contains the exact response envelope and outcome. It is written after the marker. Replaying a request returns this record; absence of a response never makes a committed marker invisible. * Business records include RoomMessage, SeqHead, SendManifest, Attempt, GrantRecord, ApprovalRecord, WaitRecord, TicketRecord, immutable ticket events, DatasetDescriptor, DatasetRow, ReportEnvelope, and AuditRecord. * `TombstoneRecord` is a committed version with `state=tombstone`; it suppresses older versions but is itself retained until the configured retention boundary.
A business record is **committed** only through a valid marker. Readers must ignore an otherwise well-formed append with no marker, a marker whose intent/constituent list does not match, a marker with a missing or mismatching constituent, a marker from a stale fence, and any record whose schema version is unsupported. No reader may expose a prepared record or an uncommitted marker.

## G.3 Key grammar and namespaces
All canonical keys have a leading slash. IDs match `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9._-]*`; room IDs are `(obj|task|space)-[a-z0-9-]+`; decimal sequence components are zero-padded. These are keys, not filesystem paths, and are validated before allocation.
TABLE 7.1-2 — G.3 Key grammar and namespaces
| Family | Canonical key | |---|---| | request claim | `/chd/request/<request-id>` | | journal intent | `/chd/journal/<tx-id>/intent` | | journal constituent receipt | `/chd/journal/<tx-id>/step/<step:03d>` | | commit marker | `/chd/journal/<tx-id>/commit` | | response | `/chd/response/<request-id>` | | writer lease mirror | `/chd/system/writer` | | room/head/message | `/chd/room/<room-id>/_head`, `/chd/room/<room-id>/m<seq:012d>` | | send/attempt/manifest | `/chd/send/<send-id>/manifest`, `/chd/send/<send-id>/attempt/<attempt-id>` | | ticket/event | `/chd/ticket/<ticket-id>`, `/chd/ticket/<ticket-id>/event/m<seq:012d>` | | grant/audit | `/chd/grant/<grant-id>`, `/chd/audit/<audit-seq:012d>` | | dataset/row/publication | `/chd/dataset/<send-id>/<dataset-id>`, `/chd/dataset/<send-id>/<dataset-id>/r<row:08d>`, `/chd/dataset/<send-id>/<dataset-id>/publication` | | archive | `/sessions/<agent>/<profile>/<session-id>/<checkpoint-id>/manifest`, `/gaps/<agent>/<profile>/<session-id>/<checkpoint-id>` |
The complete regexes live in `schemas/keys.yaml`. Reserved segments are `_head`, `intent`, `step`, `commit`, `publication`, and `manifest`; user IDs may not equal a reserved segment. A malformed key, namespace mismatch, or sequence-width mismatch returns `invalid_key` before `RequestClaim` is written.

## G.4 Durable compound-write protocol
There is no claim that multiple DuckBrain appends are atomic. The following protocol gives an observable commit boundary using only individually durable writes and a last-written marker. `step` numbers are fixed by the operation contract, not allocated from wall time.
1. **Claim.** Validate identity, authorization, schema, CAS, and the request digest. Append `RequestClaim(state=claimed, request_digest, operation, tx_id)`. If the claim already exists, compare bytes: equal returns the existing transaction; different bytes return `duplicate_identity_conflict`. A claim is not business visibility. 2. **Intent.** Append `JournalIntent(state=prepared, tx_id, request_id, fence_epoch, constituent list, expected digests, preconditions)`. The list is complete before step 2 ends. Every retry uses the same `tx_id` and list. 3. **Constituents.** For each step in declared order, append the canonical business record with `state=prepared`, `tx_id`, and `write_id=tx_id/step`. Read it back. A retry of the same `(tx_id, step, digest)` returns the original receipt; a different digest refuses with `idempotency_conflict`. The controller never advances to the next step after an uncertain readback. 4. **Commit marker.** After all constituent readbacks match the intent, append exactly one `CommitMarker(state=committed)` last, then fsync and read it back. This is the only transition that makes the listed constituents visible. The marker's digest covers the ordered list and all constituent digests. 5. **Response.** Append `ResponseRecord(state=returned)` containing the exact response and all committed record references. Read it back, then return it. If response append/readback is uncertain, the committed marker remains authoritative and a retry returns the same response reconstructed from the marker. 6. **Wake/external effect.** Only after marker and response readback may the controller wake a scheduler, gateway, Crier, or client. External calls carry `request_id`, `tx_id`, and their own dedupe key. Their response is never folded into the store commit.
For a single-key operation the intent, business record, marker, and response still exist. This uniformity makes restart repair and idempotency testable. A failed constituent leaves the transaction `pending` or `aborted`; it never produces a partial success. If a marker is not provably committed, readers hide every prepared constituent.

### G.4.1 Operation-specific constituent order
* **Room append:** request claim → intent → head reservation → message → request/dedupe receipt → audit → marker → response. The head reservation is durable before the message; an unused reserved tail is a permanent gap and is never reused. * **Manifest/admission:** request claim → intent → manifest/attempt → reservation/grant receipt → audit → marker → response. No wake or external POST precedes the marker. * **Grant/approval:** request claim → intent → grant or approval → audit → marker → response. Denial writes a denial audit in its own committed transaction; it is not a successful revision. * **Ticket mutation:** request claim → intent → TicketRecord revision → ticket event → required link/index records → audit → marker → response. A stale CAS stops before any constituent. * **Report/message:** request claim → intent → ReportEnvelope → room message → freshness/dedupe receipt → audit → marker → response. * **Dataset publish:** request claim → intent → DatasetDescriptor(staging) → all typed dense DatasetRow records → count/digest receipt → publication marker → audit → commit marker → response. The publication marker is itself a constituent and is unreadable until the outer commit marker validates; `published` is never inferred from row presence.

## G.5 Explicit failure and unknown-outcome table
The normative fault-injection register is `tables/crash-windows.csv`. It covers each constituent, including request claim, message, head, manifest, grant, audit, ticket event, dataset row, and publication marker. The common rule after a fault is: stop, reacquire or verify the fence, read claim/intent/steps/marker, and classify `committed`, `pending`, `aborted`, or `unknown`.
TABLE 7.1-3 — G.5 Explicit failure and unknown-outcome table
| Fault after write attempt | Required result and next action | |---|---| | Request claim | If exact claim readback exists, reuse `tx_id`; if absent, retry claim; if authority cannot distinguish, return `request_outcome_unknown` and do not allocate a second transaction. | | Journal intent | Read the intent by `tx_id`; mismatching list/digest is `integrity_journal_conflict`; no constituent or wake is allowed. | | Head | If exact head reservation exists, retain its range and never reuse it; if uncertain, scan the head and messages, then refuse allocation until the range is resolved. | | Message | Exact `(room, seq, request_id, digest)` replays; missing message may be appended at the same reserved key; different bytes are `duplicate_identity_conflict`. | | Manifest | Read the effective manifest by `send_id/attempt_id`; retry the same revision only; unknown external execution remains held and no second POST occurs. | | Grant | Read lineage and grant digest; equal retry replays; an unknown authority write blocks the protected action and never implies approval. | | Audit | Rebuild the expected audit digest from intent. Missing audit prevents marker completion; a committed marker with missing audit is corruption and stops the affected scope. | | Ticket event | Check record/event sequence and `tx_id`; equal retry replays; a record without its event is not visible as the transition and is repaired by a new revision, never by editing history. | | Dataset row | Leave descriptor staging; retry the same row key/digest or mark staging failed. No row is queryable until publication and outer marker. | | Publication marker | Read descriptor, rows, and marker. If marker absent, dataset remains staging/failed; if present but outer marker absent, hide it; only matching committed markers publish. | | Commit marker | A marker readback miss is `unknown`; reconcile all listed steps. If every step is durable and no conflicting marker exists, retry the same marker bytes; otherwise leave pending and refuse response/wake. | | Response | Reconstruct from the valid marker and write/replay the same response; never create another business transaction. |
An error after any constituent is returned with a stable code and `retryable` flag. `retryable` means retry the same `request_id`, `tx_id`, step, and digest, never generate new IDs. Errors include `fence_lost`, `durability_unconfirmed`, `readback_mismatch`, `journal_incomplete`, `integrity_equal_rev_conflict`, `request_outcome_unknown`, and `external_outcome_unknown`.

## G.6 Writer exclusion and fencing
The controller has one logical writer at a time. `LeaseAuthority` owns lease name `chd/controller`; the durable `WriterLease` mirror is descriptive and cannot itself grant a lease. `owner_id` is a stable deployment/controller identity; `boot_id` is a fresh cryptographic random value per process start; `fence_epoch` is a strictly increasing lease-service value.
* **Acquire/startup race:** call linearizable `AcquireOrRenew(name, owner_id, boot_id, ttl)`. Acquisition succeeds only if no unexpired owner exists, or the service's conditional takeover increments `fence_epoch`. Two simultaneous starters can receive at most one success. The loser enters `writer_lease_held` and writes no business state. * **Renewal:** renew before `ttl/3`, with a monotonic local deadline and a bounded clock-skew margin. Wall-clock time is not authority. A failed or late renewal immediately sets the process `uncertain`, stops allocations, external calls, and all writes, and attempts a read-only reconciliation. * **Takeover:** a replacement may take over only after the lease authority proves expiry and atomically installs a new `boot_id` and `fence_epoch`. It writes a committed takeover incident, then runs recovery before readiness. Lease expiry by itself never proves the old process stopped. * **Stale-writer refusal:** `FencedStore` rejects every append whose owner/boot/epoch is not the current lease tuple. A paused old process therefore cannot write after takeover, even if it wakes before noticing its local timer. The old process must exit or remain read-only. * **Uncertain authority:** if LeaseAuthority or FencedStore cannot answer whether the tuple is current, the controller refuses startup/continuation with `writer_lease_held_or_unknown` or `fencing_unavailable`; it does not guess from a timestamp, process list, or expired local TTL. * **Release:** voluntary release is a conditional compare-and-set on the exact tuple and is followed by readback. A lost release response is unknown; the owner does not retry with a new boot identity and a successor waits for authority resolution/expiry.
Every append, marker, and response carries the fence tuple. Recovery verifies that no record was accepted with a stale fence. A store implementation that cannot enforce this at the write boundary is unsupported for CHD single-controller mode.

## G.7 Version resolution, tombstones, and visibility
A logical state key may have many append-only versions. The reader fetches all candidate versions within the scan boundary, discards unsupported schema and records not covered by a valid commit marker, then groups by canonical key. It selects the greatest `(rev, commit_seq, record_id)` only after checking all records at the greatest `rev`:
1. If equal-revision canonical bytes are identical, retain one deterministic copy (lowest `record_id`) and record duplicate count. 2. If equal-revision bytes differ, return `integrity_equal_rev_conflict`, create a corruption incident if the writer is available, and expose no value. 3. A highest valid tombstone hides the logical key and all older values. An older live value may not be resurrected because a tombstone was compacted or omitted. 4. A prepared/staged version without a valid commit marker is invisible. For datasets, only a descriptor with committed publication marker and complete row count/digest is queryable. 5. A record newer than the running schema is `schema_version_unsupported`, not silently skipped to an older version.
Room reads use `(seq, message_key)` ascending; duplicate sequence values with different canonical messages are an integrity conflict. Ticket events use sequence ascending and require contiguous committed event prefixes; reserved room sequence gaps are legal only when represented by a head reservation. All other scans use declared `(order_column, record_id)` ascending. Timestamps never break ties or determine freshness.

## G.8 Complete scans and restart-safe cursors
A query starts with an authoritative `SnapshotToken` containing namespace, prefix, selected fields/order, `high_water_commit_seq`, schema epoch, and expiry. `high_water_commit_seq` is captured before the first page; records committed later are excluded and belong to a later query. If the substrate cannot return a snapshot token and high-water in one authoritative read, the query fails `snapshot_unavailable` rather than claiming completeness.
The controller then loops each backing call until its continuation is null:
1. Request `page_size <= backing_page_limit` with prefix, snapshot token, and opaque continuation. 2. Reject a malformed page, a repeated cursor, a cursor that moves backwards, or a page whose item count exceeds the requested limit as `scan_incomplete`; do not return partial success. 3. Append items to the accumulator, verify each item is within prefix and `commit_seq <= high_water`, and advance only with the server continuation token. Never emulate continuation with offsets. 4. When continuation is null, resolve versions/tombstones and deduplicate. For a query spanning multiple prefixes, complete each prefix and merge by the declared order plus stable tie-breaker. 5. Emit `next_cursor` containing snapshot hash, high-water, order, and the last emitted tuple. A resumed query reuses the same snapshot until expiry; an expired/invalid cursor returns `cursor_expired` and restarts a new snapshot. It never silently changes the window. 6. If a page is lost after the caller received it, resuming from its cursor is safe because the tuple is exclusive. If the caller has no cursor, restart from the beginning and deduplicate by canonical key/record identity; never skip based on a guessed offset.
The result is complete only when every backing prefix returned `continuation=null` and all eligible records through the high-water were resolved. A scan over more than one backing page must prove this loop in evidence; one successful page is not a complete query.

## G.9 Recovery and repair
Startup state is `recovering`, never `ready`. After acquiring a fresh fence, recovery scans requests/intents/steps/markers/responses, then heads/messages, manifests/attempts, tickets/events, grants/audits, datasets/publications, bonds/waits, and archive gaps. It verifies marker coverage, canonical digests, equal-revision integrity, monotone revisions, event prefixes, and fence validity. It rebuilds worklists only from valid committed records.
* A valid marker with a missing response is replayed/repaired with the original response. * An intent with all steps durable but no marker retries the same marker only after current-fence verification; if any step conflicts, the transaction is quarantined. * An intent with incomplete steps is resumed at the first missing step only when no external effect could have occurred; otherwise it is `unknown` and held for reconciliation. * A marker/constituent mismatch, equal-revision conflict, stale-fence append, or impossible event sequence stops the affected scope, writes an incident if possible, and pages. Recovery never deletes history, rewinds revisions, fills a room gap, or chooses a conflict winner. * Unknown gateway/scheduler/Crier outcomes retain capacity and do not trigger a second external action. Release requires verified, correlated provider/runtime terminal evidence committed with readback and audit. An operator statement, ordinary report or process absence is not a substitute; the concrete producer/schema remains G-06.
Readiness is published only after lease/fencing, store fsync/readback, recovery scans, and all mandatory gates pass. A controller with uncertain authority may provide read-only status but must refuse mutation and dispatch.

## G.10 Query contracts The required internal SnapshotToken adapter returns `{snapshot, items, next_cursor, complete}`; this is not the native DuckBrain HTTP list shape and not a replacement for operation-specific controller response envelopes in `contracts/openapi.yaml`. `complete` is true only after the continuation loop and version resolution finish. Exact reads return the highest valid committed version or a named integrity/schema error. Q1–Q9 in `queries/cookbook.md` are executable-shaped examples; Q6 and Q8 specifically demonstrate typed published dataset scans and equal-revision refusal. The acceptance suite must inject faults at every row in `tables/crash-windows.csv`, race two startup acquisitions, pause an owner through expiry and attempt a stale append, scan more than one backing page for every family, inject a tombstone and equal-revision conflict, and assert that no uncommitted marker or prepared record is returned.
